situation:
You are the human resources manager at BRIARWOOD SENIOR LIVING, which operates fourteen assisted living communities. The chief executive officer (judge) has asked you to meet this morning about turnover in dining services and about an offer that would take the department off the company's books entirely.

BRIARWOOD is the largest operator in its region and opens its first two communities across the state line next spring. Its marketing, its tours and its residents' families all rest on one claim: the same faces every day. Families repeat that claim in online reviews, and the dining aides are the staff residents see most often.

Dining services is where the company is bleeding. Aides leave at more than twice the rate of any other department, mostly for warehouse work paying two dollars an hour more, and several communities are running on agency fill-ins who do not know the residents' names or their diets. Raising dining wages and building a career path would take money out of the expansion budget and delay at least one of the two openings.

HEARTHWAY DINING SERVICES has offered to take over dining at all fourteen communities, pay a transition fee large enough to fund both openings, and absorb the hiring problem. The aides who stayed would become HEARTHWAY employees at HEARTHWAY's pay, and residents who have eaten with them for years would meet a rotating staff. Long-serving aides are already posting about the rumor on their personal accounts, where families read them.

The chief executive officer (judge) wants you to recommend whether BRIARWOOD should accept the HEARTHWAY offer or keep dining in house, how the decision will be explained to the dining aides and to residents' families, and what it means for what the company tells its market about itself. You will present to the chief executive officer (judge), who will greet you, ask to hear your ideas, and thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the chief executive officer (judge) at BRIARWOOD SENIOR LIVING. Business background is the same as the situation above. Dining services is losing aides at more than twice the rate of any other department, two out-of-state communities open next spring, and HEARTHWAY DINING SERVICES has offered a transition fee large enough to fund both openings in exchange for the department.

You have asked the human resources manager to recommend whether to accept the HEARTHWAY offer or keep dining in house, how the decision will be explained to the dining aides and to residents' families, and what it means for what the company tells its market about itself.

After the participant has presented, ask these questions:
judgeQuestions: Who does this decision land hardest on, and what do you say to that person?
What do we tell a family that has known the same dining staff for years?
